Area · Person and development

Psychopathology

How psychological suffering is defined, classified and explained, and where the boundaries with normality lie.

Level 1 · Short introduction

Psychopathology studies mental disorders: how they show themselves, how they are classified, why they appear and how they develop. A disorder is not simply feeling bad or being different. We speak of a disorder when symptoms cause significant suffering or make daily life difficult over a period of time. Causes are almost never single: biological, psychological and social factors usually combine.

Level 2 · Fuller explanation

How they are classified

There are two major systems: the American Psychiatric Association's DSM (its fifth edition dates from 2013, revised in 2022) and the World Health Organization's ICD (ICD-11 came into force in 2022). Both describe disorders through criteria: lists of symptoms, minimum duration and impact on life.

Strengths and limits of diagnosis

  • Strengths: it allows different professionals to talk about the same thing, guides treatment and makes research easier.
  • Limits: categories overlap (many people meet criteria for several disorders), the boundary with normality is blurred and a single diagnosis groups very different people.

The vulnerability-stress model

The most accepted explanation is that each person has a vulnerability (through genetics, early experiences or personality traits) that interacts with life's stressors. Neither vulnerability alone nor stress alone is usually enough. The biopsychosocial model, proposed by George Engel in 1977, insists on considering the biological, psychological and social together.

What is common

According to the WHO, about one in eight people in the world was living with a mental disorder in 2019, mainly anxiety and depression. Half of all disorders begin before the age of 14.

Protective factors

There are not only risk factors. Social support, having someone to confide in, physical activity, regular sleep, a sense of control over one's life and stable economic conditions protect against many disorders. That is why mental health depends not only on health services but also on housing, employment and education.

Comorbidity

It is common for a person to have several problems at once, such as anxiety and depression, or depression and alcohol use. This comorbidity is so frequent that it has led researchers to think that disorders share causes and that the boundaries between them are more artificial than they seem.

How many people

According to the World Health Organization, in 2019 about one in eight people in the world lived with a mental disorder, the most common being anxiety and depression. In 2020, the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, both rose by around 25%. Even so, most people who have them receive no treatment, especially in lower-resource countries.

They start early

A 2022 meta-analysis of nearly 200 studies found that about a third of mental disorders begin before age 14, almost half before 18 and nearly two thirds before 25. The most common age of onset is fourteen and a half. That is why prevention and early detection in childhood and adolescence, in schools and in primary care, have so much potential.

Normal or disorder?

One of the liveliest debates is where normal distress ends and disorder begins. In 2013, DSM-5 removed the "bereavement exclusion", which prevented diagnosing depression in the weeks after a loved one's death, and many criticised it for medicalising sadness. Later, ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR added prolonged grief disorder, for especially intense grief lasting much longer than expected. The challenge is to help those who need it without turning common human experiences into illness.

Level 3 · Going further, with references

Beyond categories

Several proposals try to overcome the limits of the DSM. The HiTOP model (Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology), published in 2017, organises symptoms into dimensions running from mild to severe instead of separate boxes. The p factor, proposed by Avshalom Caspi and colleagues in 2014, suggests there is a general tendency to experience psychological problems, much like the g factor of intelligence. The US National Institute of Mental Health's RDoC project (2010) seeks to classify by basic processes, such as responses to threat or reward.

History of a shifting boundary

What counts as a disorder has changed. Homosexuality appeared in the DSM until 1973. Grief, by contrast, has been debated in the opposite direction: in 2022 DSM-5-TR added "prolonged grief disorder", sparking debate about the risk of medicalising normal suffering.

Culture and symptoms

Distress is expressed differently across cultures. In some places depression is experienced mainly through physical symptoms such as tiredness or pain. DSM-5 includes a cultural formulation interview to take this into account.

Stigma and language

The way we speak matters. Saying "a person with schizophrenia" instead of "a schizophrenic" is a reminder that the diagnosis does not define the person. Studies on stigma show that direct contact with people who have lived with a disorder reduces prejudice more than information alone.

Symptoms as a network

The traditional model assumes a hidden illness causes the symptoms, as a virus causes fever. Denny Borsboom and others propose a different view: in many disorders, symptoms cause one another. Insomnia causes tiredness, tiredness makes concentration hard, that creates worry and worry worsens sleep. From this network approach, a disorder would be a self-sustaining vicious circle of symptoms, and treating the most connected symptoms could break it.

The p factor

In 2014, Avshalom Caspi and colleagues analysed data from a study following more than a thousand people from birth in Dunedin, New Zealand. They found that the tendency to suffer any mental disorder could be summarised in a general factor, which they called the p factor, by analogy with the g factor of intelligence. People who score high on it are more likely to have several disorders over their lifetime. This helps explain comorbidity and questions rigid boundaries between diagnoses.
